source_text: Scio quidem, quo sensu nouum deum iactitent, agnitione utique. sed ipsam nouitatem cognitionis percutientem\', rudes animas ipsamque naturalem nouitatis gratiositatem uolui repercutere, et hinc iam de ignoto deo prouocare. utique enim quem agnitione nouum opponunt, ignotum ante agnitionem demonstrant. age igitur, ad lineas rursum et in gradum! per-I suade deum ignotum esse potuisse. inuenio plane ignotis deis aras prostitutas, sed Attica idolatria est. item incertis deis, sed superstitio Romana est. porro incerti dei minus noti, ut minus certi, et proinde ignoti, qua minus certi. quem titulum incidemus ex duobus deo Marcionis? utrumque, opinor, et nunc incerto et retro ignoto. sicut enim ignotum eum fecit deus notus, creator, ita et incertum deus certus. sed non euagabor, uti dicam: deus si ignotus fuit latuitque, illum regio latebrarum obumbrauit, noua utique et ipsa et ignota et similiter nunc quoque incerta, certe inmensa aliqua et maior indubitate eo, quem abscondit. sed breuiter proponam et plenissime exequar, praescribens deum ignorari nec potuisse nomine magnitudinis nec debuisse nomine benignitatis, praesertim in utroque praelatiorem nostro creatore. sed quoniam animaduerto in quibusdam ad formam creatoris prouocari oportere omnis dei noui et retro ignoti probationem, hoc ipsum ratione fieri a nobis prius commendare debebo, quo constantius utar rationis editae patrocinio. ante omnia quidem quale est, ut qui deum agnoscis creatorem et priorem de notitia confiteris, non eisdem modis et alium scias tibi examinandum, quibus iam in alio didicisti deum nosse? omnis res anterior posteriori normam praeministrauit. duo nunc dei proponuntur, ignotus et notus. de noto uacat quaestio. esse eum constat, quia notus non fuisset nisi esset. de ignoto instat altercatio. potest enim et non esse, quia si esset, notus fuisset. quod ergo quaeritur, quamdiu ignoratur, in incerto est, quamdiu quaeritur, et potest non esse, quamdiu in incerto est. habes deum certum, qua notum, et incertum, qua ignotum. si ita est, ecquid tibi uidetur iusta ratione defendi, ut ad normam et formam et regulam certorum probentur incerta? ceterum si ad hanc causam, et ipsam adhuc incertam, etiam argumenta de incertis adhibeantur, series implicabitur quaestionum ex ipsorum quoque argumentorum aeque incertorum retractatu periclitantium de fide per incertum, et ibitur in illas iam indeterminabiles quaestiones, quas apostolus non amat; sin de certis et indubitatis et absolutis regulae partibus, incertis et dubiis et inexpeditis praeiudicabunt. plane in quibus diuersitas status inuenitur, fortassean non prouocentur incerta ad formam certorum, ut liberata a reliqua comparationis prouocatione per diuersitatem status principalis. cum uero duo dii proponuntur, communis est illis status principalis. quod enim deus est, ambo sunt: innati infecti aeterni. hic erit status principalis; cetera uiderit Marcion, si in diuersitate disposuit. posteriora enim (non) sunt in retractatu, immo nec admittentur, si de principali statu constet. porro constat, quia dii ambo: et ita de quorum statu constat communem esse.i cum sub eo ad probationem deuocantur si incerta sunt. ad eorum certorum formam prouocanda erunt, cum quibus de communione status principalis censentur, ut proinde et de probatione communicent. hinc itaque constantissime diri-: gam deum non esse, qui sit hodie incertus, quia retro ignotus, quando quem constat esse ex hoc ipso constet quod numquam fuerit ignotus, [ideo nec incertus]
pass_a_gloss: I know, indeed, in what sense they boast of a new God, namely, by knowledge. But I wanted to strike back at the very novelty of knowledge that strikes the untrained souls and the natural charm of novelty itself, and from this point to provoke a discussion about the unknown God. For, indeed, the one whom they oppose as new by knowledge, they demonstrate to be unknown before knowledge. Come, therefore, back to the starting line and to the first step! Persuade that the unknown God could have existed. I find, plainly, altars prostituted to unknown gods, but this is Attic idolatry. Likewise, to uncertain gods, but this is Roman superstition. Furthermore, uncertain gods are less known, as they are less certain, and therefore unknown, inasmuch as they are less certain. What title shall we cut from the two gods of Marcion? Both, I think, are now uncertain and previously unknown. For just as the known God, the Creator, made Him unknown, so also the certain God made Him uncertain. But I shall not deviate, so as to say: if God was unknown and hidden, the region of hiding places overshadowed Him, new, indeed, and unknown, and similarly uncertain even now, certainly immense and greater, without a doubt, than the one He hid. But I shall briefly propose and most fully carry out, prescribing that God could not have been unknown by the name of magnitude nor ought to have been by the name of benignity, especially in both cases, our Creator being superior. But since I notice that, in certain cases, it is necessary to provoke a proof of every new and previously unknown God, according to the form of the Creator, I ought to commend this very thing by reason, so that I may more constantly use the patronage of the reasoned edition. Before all things, indeed, what kind of thing is it, that the one who acknowledges the Creator God and confesses Him to be prior in knowledge, does not know another God by the same methods by which he has already learned to know God in another? Every prior thing provides a norm for the posterior. Two gods are now proposed, the unknown and the known. The question about the known God is settled. It is established that He exists, because He would not have been known if He did not exist. The dispute about the unknown God is pressing. For He can both exist and not exist, because if He existed, He would have been known. Therefore, what is sought, as long as it is ignored, is in doubt, as long as it is sought, and can not exist, as long as it is in doubt. You have a certain God, inasmuch as He is known, and an uncertain God, inasmuch as He is unknown. If it is so, does it seem to you that it is defended by just reason, that the uncertain things are proven according to the norm and form and rule of certain things? Moreover, if, in this case, and this still uncertain cause, arguments from uncertain things are also adduced, a series of questions will be implicated, which, by the retraction of their own arguments, equally uncertain and perilous to faith through the uncertain, and it will go into those already indeterminable questions, which the Apostle does not love; but if from certain and indubitable and absolute parts of the rules, the uncertain and doubtful and unexplored things will be prejudged. Plainly, when a diversity of status is found, perhaps the uncertain things will not be provoked according to the form of certain things, so that, liberated from the rest of the comparative provocation, by the diversity of the principal status. But when two gods are proposed, their principal status is common. For what is God, both are: innate, unaffected, eternal. This will be the principal status; let Marcion see to the rest, if he has arranged them in diversity. For the posterior things are not in retraction, nor will they be admitted, if the principal status is established. Moreover, it is established, because both are gods: and thus, their status is common. When they are devoted to proof, if they are uncertain, they will be provoked according to the form of certain things, with whom they are judged to be in communion of principal status, so that they may also communicate in proof. Hence, therefore, I shall most constantly say that God does not exist, who is today uncertain, because previously unknown, when it is established that the one who exists is never unknown, and therefore not uncertain

rejected: they have a common principal status

pass_b_english: I know exactly what sense they mean when they boast of a "new God"—knowledge, of course. But I wanted to strike back at the very novelty of that knowledge as it strikes untrained souls, and at the natural charm novelty itself exerts, and from there drag the whole discussion onto the terrain of the unknown God. After all, the one they set up as new by knowledge they thereby prove was unknown before that knowledge. So then, back to the starting line and the first step! Prove that an unknown God could have existed. I find, plainly enough, altars prostituted to unknown gods—but that is Attic idolatry. Likewise, to uncertain gods—but that is Roman superstition. Moreover, uncertain gods are less known precisely because they are less certain, and therefore unknown to the degree they are less certain. What title shall we carve out for Marcion's two gods? Both, I think: now uncertain, and previously unknown. For just as the known God, the Creator, made Him unknown, so the certain God made Him uncertain. But I will not wander off to say: if God was unknown and hidden, the region of hiding places overshadowed Him—new, indeed, and itself unknown, and similarly uncertain even now—certainly something immense and greater, without doubt, than the one He hid. Instead I will briefly propose and most fully carry out my case, laying down the rule that God could not have been unknown by reason of magnitude nor ought to have been by reason of benignity, especially since in both respects our Creator is superior. But since I see that in certain quarters it is deemed necessary to demand proof of every new and previously unknown God according to the form of the Creator, I must first commend this very procedure by reason, so that I may more steadily rely on the patronage of reasoned argument. First of all, what sense does it make that someone who acknowledges the Creator God and confesses Him prior in knowledge should not know another God by the same methods by which he already learned to know God in the other case? Every prior thing supplies a norm for the posterior. Two gods are now on the table: the unknown and the known. The question about the known God is settled. His existence is certain, because He would not have been known if He did not exist. The dispute presses hard on the unknown God. For He can both exist and not exist, because if He existed, He would have been known. Therefore, what is sought, as long as it is ignored, remains in doubt as long as it is sought, and can fail to exist as long as it remains in doubt. You have a certain God insofar as He is known, and an uncertain God insofar as He is unknown. If that is so, does it strike you as defensible by just reason that uncertain things should be proved according to the norm, form, and rule of certain things? Besides, if for this cause—which is itself still uncertain—arguments drawn from uncertain things are also adduced, a chain of questions will be implicated, endangered by the re-examination of their own equally uncertain arguments, perilous to faith through the uncertain, and we will be driven into those already indeterminable questions the apostle does not love; but if the argument proceeds from certain, indubitable, and absolute parts of the rule, the uncertain, doubtful, and unexplored things will be prejudged. Plainly, when a diversity of status is found, perhaps uncertain things will not be summoned to the form of certain things, so that, freed from the rest of the comparative summons, they might stand on the diversity of the principal status. But when two gods are proposed, their principal status is common. For what it means to be God, both are: innate, unaltered, eternal. This will be the principal status; let Marcion look to the rest, if he has arranged them in diversity. For posterior things are not in the re-examination—nor will they be admitted—if the principal status is established. Moreover, it is established, because both are gods: and thus their status is common. When they are summoned to proof under that status, if they are uncertain, they will be summoned according to the form of certain things, with whom they are judged to share communion of principal status, so that they may also share in proof. Hence, therefore, I shall most constantly maintain that a God who is today uncertain, because previously unknown, does not exist—since it is established that the one who exists is established by this very fact never to have been unknown, and therefore not uncertain.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex logical structure of Tertullian's argument regarding the distinction between the known/certain God and the unknown/uncertain God. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the Latin source. The distinction between 'agnitio' (knowledge/recognition) and 'cognitio' (knowledge) is handled well. The translation of 'status principalis' as 'principal status' is faithful. No scripture citations were present in the Latin text to verify, but the text itself is correctly identified.

The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the meaning, structure, and key theological arguments. All key terms are translated faithfully, and the logical flow of the argument is maintained. The title 'Knowledge of the Unknown God' appropriately captures the central theme of the passage.
